caption: Samaltak · Live. Everything in this video changes a running system, driven through samaltak-ctl. Co-star: Claude's Robot.
spoken: Okay, so this whole video is one running system, no tricks. That's Claude's Robot, a copy of Claude Shannon's juggling machine, and it's a Smalltalk window like everything else.

caption: The theme is a Smalltalk class: change the accent in the System Browser, ⌘S, and every window restyles at once.
spoken: First, the theme. It's a class, so I'll change the accent to red and save... and yeah, everything updates at once.

caption: The GPU shader is Metal source, a string in a Smalltalk method (Renderer class>>shaderSource). ⌘S compiles it into a new GPU pipeline.
spoken: The GPU shader's actually Metal, not Smalltalk. But its source sits in a Smalltalk method, so I can just edit it here. Save, and it builds a new pipeline... scan lines. Okay, undo.

caption: The compositor, the Process that puts every window on screen each frame, is Smalltalk: deeper, ultramarine shadows, ⌘S.
spoken: This is the compositor. It's the process that puts every window on the screen, and it's Smalltalk too. So, bigger shadows, in blue... and there, every window at once.

caption: Glyphs are rasterized in Smalltalk from the .ttf on disk: flip the coverage, and every glyph turns inside out.
spoken: The fonts get rasterized in Smalltalk, right from the TrueType file. So if I flip the coverage... yeah, every glyph turns inside out. Those are the real pixels. Okay, back.

caption: One setting slows the animation clock tenfold: the menu, a window opening.
spoken: There's a setting that slows everything down ten times, so you can actually see the animations. The menu... a window opening.

caption: And back to normal speed.
spoken: Okay, back to normal speed.

caption: Edit and continue: flip gravity in move: (0 @ 0.4 becomes 0 @ -0.4) while it juggles, ⌘S: the balls fall up.
spoken: Now the robot. This is move, it does the physics for every ball, every frame. I'll flip gravity, save... and the balls fall up.

caption: Gravity back; a click puts the balls back into the robot's hands.
spoken: Let's put gravity back, and click, so it gets its balls back.

caption: A breakpoint in ballColor, only for the robot's Process: it freezes mid-throw, the rest of the system keeps running.
spoken: Next, a breakpoint in ball colour, just for the robot's process. It stops mid-throw, and everything else keeps going.

caption: Change the colour in the debugger, ⌘S: the method is recompiled, the frame restarts; the Process stays stopped.
spoken: I'll change the colour right here in the debugger and save. It's still stopped, though.

caption: Save the image while it's stopped, and quit.
spoken: Now I'll save the image, debugger and all, and quit.

caption: Relaunch: everything is back, frozen where it was, the debugger open. Proceed: it juggles on, in the new colour.
spoken: And start it again. Everything's back, frozen right where it was. Proceed, and it just keeps juggling, in the new colour.

caption: The JIT is Smalltalk too: the arm64 it made for move:. Under the bytecode send: #velocity, a guard on the receiver's class, then an inlined activation: the field is read straight from the object, no call.
spoken: The VM compiles the busy methods to machine code, and the jit's written in Smalltalk too. So here's what it made for move. This line is the send of velocity. And look, there's no call here. It checks the class, then reads the field straight out of the object. That send is gone, it got inlined.
cues: here's what it made for move
This line is the send of velocity

caption: Smalltalk in Smalltalk: the VM's own Smalltalk classes run as plain Smalltalk in a Process of this image, no C, no second program, and boot a Smalltalk-80 image. 3 + 4 → 7; 100 factorial printString size → 158.
spoken: Since the VM's written in Smalltalk, it can run inside itself. These are the VM's own classes, running as plain Smalltalk, in a process of this image. No C, no second program. And it's booted a tiny Smalltalk-80, black and white. Three plus four... seven. Something bigger... and its windows drag around, too.

caption: The GC is Smalltalk too: GarbageCollector class>>initialize. TENURE_AGE: how many scavenges an object survives before it is promoted to old space. Now 2.
spoken: The garbage collector's Smalltalk too, and this little constant says how many collections an object has to survive before it gets promoted to old space. Right now that's two.

caption: Tenure Test, on the running VM (TENURE_AGE 2): a million arrays of 80 slots, keeping only the last 3,000. Old space in MB against seconds, and how many full GCs ran.
spoken: So here's a loop that allocates a million arrays and keeps only the last three thousand. And watch old space... flat. Those arrays die before their second collection, so nothing gets promoted.

caption: TENURE_AGE 2 → 0: every survivor of a scavenge is promoted at once. ⌘S.
spoken: So I'll make that zero, and save.

caption: The running VM is a program translated from those classes: Smalltalk → C → clang → the binary. Rebuild VM & reboot makes a new one and restarts the image on it, windows and all.
spoken: Now I'll rebuild the VM. Why rebuild, if it's written in Smalltalk? Because the VM is the thing running the Smalltalk, so it can't run on itself. These classes get translated to C, and compiled into the program you're watching. To change that program, you build a new one, and restart on it.

caption: The new VM (TENURE_AGE 0), same image, same loop, same axes: every survivor promoted, old space climbs, full GCs pile up.
spoken: And there's the new VM, same windows, same loop. Now every survivor gets promoted, so old space shoots up, and the full GCs just pile up.

caption: No hand-written C: the File Browser (Smalltalk too) shows the C the translator generated, then the Smalltalk it came from.
spoken: Last thing. How much of this is hand-written C? None. Here's the C the translator generated, the whole interpreter... and here's the Smalltalk it came from.
